transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you in today?

I guess… what brings me in is that I can’t stop noticing my face, especially this droop around my mouth and jaw. It looks uneven to me in every photo, every mirror, even shop windows sometimes. People say I look fine, but I don’t understand how they don’t see it.

And it’s started interfering with work. I’m an architect, so I’m supposed to be in front of clients, giving presentations, talking through designs, and lately I’ve been avoiding that when I can because I feel like they’re staring at that part of my face. It sounds vain, I know, but it feels really obvious to me.
Do you find yourself spending a lot of time thinking about the appearance of your face, maybe checking it in mirrors or photos frequently, or trying to hide it from others?

Yes… yes, I do. Before work, especially if I have a client meeting, I can lose hours in the bathroom. I’ll check the mirror, then take pictures on my phone from different angles, because the mirror feels like it lies sometimes, but then the photos are worse.

And if there’s a family event, it’s the same thing. I’ll redo my makeup, adjust a scarf around my neck or jawline, ask my husband, “Does my face look lopsided?”—and he’ll say no, but then I don’t really believe him. Then I end up scrolling through photos of other women, just comparing, which is ridiculous because I’ll start with maybe looking at hairstyles or makeup and suddenly I’m zooming in on everyone’s jawline. It just eats up so much time.

Do you ever find yourself repeating certain behaviors, like checking your face over and over, or do you feel driven to do certain things like adjust your scarf or makeup a certain way because it feels like you have to?

Yes, I do. It’s like once I start, I can’t just check once and leave it alone. Before work, or if we’re going to some family thing, I’ll be in the bathroom for ages—hours sometimes—looking in the mirror, then taking pictures on my phone from the side, from below, from… ridiculous angles, really.

And then I’ll redo my makeup, move my scarf around my jaw, take it off, put it back on. My husband will be waiting by the door and I’ll ask him again, “Does my face look lopsided?” even though I already asked. He says no, but then I think he’s just trying to get us out of the house.

Then I end up on my phone looking at photos of other women, comparing their faces to mine, which I know isn’t helpful. I’ll tell myself I’m just checking how bad it looks, but it can take over the whole morning.
